```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 6.2, fig.height = 2.3, fig.align = "center")
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

pop <- read.csv("/Users/ndtltd/Documents/Projects/Assigment K P/world_population.csv", check.names = FALSE)
## pop <- read.csv("Documents/Projects/Assignment K P/world_population.csv", check.names = FALSE)
## "/Users/ndtltd/Documents/Projects/Assigment K P
co2_raw <- read.csv("/Users/ndtltd/Documents/Projects/Assigment K P/CO2_emission.csv", check.names = FALSE)
## co2_raw <- read.csv("datasets/CO2_emission.csv", check.names = FALSE)
co2 <- co2_raw[, !duplicated(names(co2_raw)), drop = FALSE]
names(co2)[names(co2) == "Country Name"] <- "country_source"
names(co2)[names(co2) == "country_code"] <- "code"
pop_names <- data.frame(code = pop$CCA3,
                        country_name = pop[["Country/Territory"]])
co2 <- dplyr::left_join(co2, pop_names, by = "code",
                        suffix = c("_source", "_population"))
co2$country_name <- dplyr::coalesce(co2$country_name, co2$country_source)
names(pop)[names(pop) == "Country/Territory"] <- "country_name"
names(pop)[names(pop) == "CCA3"] <- "code"
names(pop)[names(pop) == "Continent"] <- "continent"
names(pop)[names(pop) == "2022 Population"] <- "pop_2022"
merged <- dplyr::inner_join(pop, co2, by = "country_name")
names(merged)[names(merged) == "2019"] <- "co2_2019"
complete <- merged[!is.na(merged$pop_2022) & !is.na(merged$co2_2019), ]

top10 <- pop[order(-pop$pop_2022), ][1:10, ]
top10$projected_2030 <- top10$pop_2022 *
  exp((top10[["Growth Rate"]] - 1) * 8)
missing_pop <- sum(is.na(read.csv("/Users/ndtltd/Documents/Projects/Assigment K P/world_population.csv",
                                  check.names = FALSE)))
duplicate_pop <- sum(duplicated(read.csv("/Users/ndtltd/Documents/Projects/Assigment K P/world_population.csv",
                                         check.names = FALSE)))
numeric_cols <- c("2022 Population", "Area (km²)", "Density (per km²)",
                  "Growth Rate", "World Population Percentage")
outlier_n <- vapply(numeric_cols, function(nm) {
  x <- read.csv("/Users/ndtltd/Documents/Projects/Assigment K P/world_population.csv", check.names = FALSE)[[nm]]
  q <- quantile(x, c(.25, .75), na.rm = TRUE, names = FALSE)
  sum(x < q[1] - 1.5 * diff(q) | x > q[2] + 1.5 * diff(q), na.rm = TRUE)
}, integer(1))

cor_vars <- data.frame(
  area = pop[["Area (km²)"]],
  density = pop[["Density (per km²)"]],
  growth_rate = pop[["Growth Rate"]] - 1,
  world_pct = pop[["World Population Percentage"]]
)
cor_mat <- cor(cor_vars, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
ct <- cor.test(complete$pop_2022, complete$co2_2019)
model <- lm(co2_2019 ~ log10(pop_2022), data = complete)
continent_sum <- aggregate(
  complete$co2_2019,
  by = list(continent = complete$continent),
  FUN = sum
)
continent_sum <- continent_sum[order(-continent_sum$x), ]
```

\begin{abstract}This study examines population growth and CO2 emissions using a 234-country
population dataset and a country-level emissions dataset. The population data
have no missing values or duplicate rows. Population projections to 2030 use
the exponential model and the reported growth factor converted to an annual
rate. The ten largest populations are summarized, and per-capita emissions
are compared across countries and continents. Across `r nrow(complete)`
countries with complete 2022 population and 2019 emissions data, Pearson
correlation is `r sprintf("%.3f", unname(ct$estimate))`
(`r format.pval(ct$p.value, digits = 2)`). The analysis finds that population
size alone does not explain per-capita emissions. Continent sums of
country-level per-capita values are reported as requested but are not totals
of continent emissions.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Population change can affect resource demand, while CO2 emissions also depend
on energy systems, consumption, and technology. This project describes
population patterns and investigates their relationship with CO2 emissions.
The interpretation distinguishes per-capita emissions from total emissions.

\section{Methods}
The population file has `r nrow(pop)` countries/territories and
`r ncol(read.csv("/Users/ndtltd/Documents/Projects/Assigment K P/world_population.csv", check.names = FALSE))`
variables, with selected population years from 1970 to 2022, area, density,
growth factor, and world-population share. The emissions file records annual
CO2 metric tons per capita from 1990 to 2019; its duplicate 2019 column was
removed. Country codes harmonized name variants before joining on canonical
country names. Missing 2019 emissions were excluded without imputation.
Population projection used \(N_{2030}=P\exp((g-1)8)\), where \(g\) is the
dataset's multiplicative growth factor and \(P\) is 2022 population.
Correlations use pairwise-complete observations; a log-population regression
was used to examine the cross-country association.

\section{Results}
The population dataset has `r duplicate_pop` duplicate rows and
`r missing_pop` missing values. By the 1.5-IQR rule, flagged observations
occur in 2022 population (`r outlier_n[1]`), area (`r outlier_n[2]`), density
(`r outlier_n[3]`), growth factor (`r outlier_n[4]`), and world share
(`r outlier_n[5]`). Extreme population and area values are plausible country
differences, so they were retained; missing CO2 values were excluded.

The ten most populous countries in 2022 are
`r paste(top10$country_name, collapse = ", ")`. Under a constant-rate
assumption, their 2030 projections are illustrative rather than official
forecasts. The population file provides only selected years (1990, 2000, 2010,
2015, 2020, and 2022), whereas emissions provide annual observations through
2019.

```{r projection-table}
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Country = top10$country_name,
    `2022 population` = top10$pop_2022,
    `Projected 2030` = round(top10$projected_2030)
  ),
  format = "latex",
  digits = 0,
  col.names = c("Country", "2022 population", "Projected 2030"),
  caption = "Exponential projections for the ten largest populations"
)
```

Population correlations with area, density, growth rate, and world population
share were computed numerically and visualized in the HTML analysis. The
area/world-share correlation is `r sprintf("%.3f", cor_mat["area", "world_pct"])`;
the density/world-share and growth-rate/world-share correlations are
`r sprintf("%.3f", cor_mat["density", "world_pct"])` and
`r sprintf("%.3f", cor_mat["growth_rate", "world_pct"])`, respectively. For the
complete population/emissions join, Pearson correlation between population
and 2019 per-capita emissions is `r sprintf("%.3f", unname(ct$estimate))`
(\(p=\)`r format.pval(ct$p.value, digits = 2)`); the log-population regression
has \(R^2=\)`r sprintf("%.3f", summary(model)$r.squared)`. These results do
not support a meaningful linear relationship between population size and
per-capita emissions in these data.

The requested sum of country-level per-capita emissions is highest in
`r continent_sum$continent[1]` (`r sprintf("%.2f", continent_sum$x[1])`),
third in `r continent_sum$continent[3]`
(`r sprintf("%.2f", continent_sum$x[3])`), and lowest in
`r continent_sum$continent[nrow(continent_sum)]`
(`r sprintf("%.2f", continent_sum$x[nrow(continent_sum)])`).
This sum is not total emissions; it weights a small and a large country
equally.

```{r continent-plot}
ggplot(continent_sum, aes(x = reorder(continent, x), y = x)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2878B5") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Sum of country per-capita values",
       title = "2019 CO2 indicator sums by continent") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)
```

\section{Discussion, lessons, and recommendations}

The analysis demonstrates data inspection, missing-value handling, variable
creation, visualization, and correlation/regression. Extreme population
values are genuine differences, not automatically errors. More importantly,
per-capita emissions and population totals measure different things. Future
analysis should use total national emissions or population-weighted
per-capita estimates for continent comparisons, annual population data for
trend analysis, and forecasts that quantify uncertainty rather than assuming
constant growth.

\section{Conclusion}
The 2030 projection provides a transparent scenario based on 2022 population
and recent growth factors. Population size alone is not a useful proxy for
per-capita CO2 emissions in this country-level comparison. Conclusions about
total emissions require a total-emissions measure and should not be drawn by
summing country per-capita values.
